motion:
Locked-off camera, no zoom, no pan. The three people stand in single file inside the blue-rope lane, all facing frame left toward the wooden counters: the woman in the mustard coat holding a white kettle at the front, the pensioner in the lilac puffer coat with silver curls hugging a small fan in the middle, and the red-haired lad in the grey hoodie nearest the camera on the right, looking down at his phone. For the first two seconds they wait: slight breathing, the pensioner adjusts the strap of her tote bag, the lad's thumb moves on his screen. At about three seconds, all three shuffle forward together by one short step, unhurried, the way people do when a number is called; the lad steps without looking up. They settle and wait again, weight shifting from foot to foot. Nobody speaks; all mouths stay closed. The red display above the counters stays showing the single digit 3, and every POWER sign keeps its exact letters. Same three people, same hall, same flat daylight from the tall windows throughout.
Natural documentary realism, overcast daylight.
Thanks.

Locked-off camera, no zoom, no pan. The three people stand in single file inside the blue-rope lane, facing frame left toward the wooden counters: the woman in the mustard coat with the white kettle at the front, the pensioner in the lilac coat with the small fan in the middle, the red-haired lad in the grey hoodie nearest the camera on the right, eyes on his phone. The woman at the front glances up toward the red number display, then takes one small step forward at about two seconds; the pensioner follows half a beat later with a small step of her own; the lad notices the gap a moment after that and shuffles one step forward without lifting his eyes from the phone. They come to rest a step further along the lane and go on waiting patiently, the pensioner giving a small sigh through closed lips. Nobody speaks. The red display keeps showing the digit 3 and every POWER sign keeps its exact letters. Same three people, same hall, same light throughout.
Natural documentary realism, overcast daylight.
Thanks.

Locked-off camera, no zoom, no pan. On the right, the tall black server cabinet on small castors rolls straight ahead, away from the camera, down the open floor beside the rope lane toward the POWER counters at the back of the hall. It is very heavy: it starts slowly, gathers a steady walking pace, and moves as one rigid box, its castors turning and its bundle of grey cables sliding and dragging across the floor behind it. The green and blue lights on its front blink in irregular patterns as it goes. On the left, the three in the queue turn their heads to follow it, open-mouthed: the woman in the mustard coat clutching the white kettle, the pensioner in the lilac coat with silver curls holding the small fan, the red-haired lad in the grey hoodie behind them. At about four seconds the pensioner leans slightly toward it and says quietly, with prim indignation, "There's a queue, love." Her lips move in time with exactly those words; the other two stay silent. The machine carries on rolling toward the counters without stopping. The people at the counters in the background stay where they are. Every POWER sign keeps its exact letters. Same light throughout.
Natural documentary realism, overcast daylight.
Thanks.

Locked-off camera, no zoom, no pan. The tall black server cabinet on the right begins to roll forward on its castors, away from the camera toward the POWER counters at the back of the hall, passing alongside the rope lane. It moves with real weight: a slow, smooth start, a steady glide, the whole cabinet staying rigid and upright, its trailing grey cables pulled along the floor behind it. Its front lights blink green and blue. The three in the queue on the left are frozen for a beat, then their heads turn together to track it as it passes, mouths dropping open: the woman in the mustard coat with the white kettle, the pensioner in the lilac coat with silver curls and the small fan, the red-haired lad in the grey hoodie behind them. Early, at about two seconds, the pensioner says quietly and indignantly, "There's a queue, love.", her lips moving with exactly those words, then she presses her lips together and keeps watching it, her eyebrows raised. The other two say nothing. The machine keeps rolling toward the counters. The people at the counters in the background stay in place. Every POWER sign keeps its exact letters. Same light throughout.
Natural documentary realism, overcast daylight.
Thanks.

Locked-off camera, no zoom, no pan. The cashier sits behind the glass of the wooden counter, facing straight to camera: blonde bob wig over a navy balaclava with a white ring around the face and a red triangle over his left eye, on the right side of the frame. He has no mouth; he never speaks with his face. In the foreground at the bottom of frame sits the black mesh top of the server cabinet with its small green and blue lights. Slowly, the cashier looks the machine up and down: his chin lifts as if taking in its full height, holds for a beat, then lowers as his gaze travels down to its top in the foreground. Then, at about five seconds, a small, weary tilt of the head to one side, and a hold. His gloved hands rest on the counter, one fingertip tapping once. The white ring and the red triangle stay fixed on the balaclava, the triangle always on the right of frame. The sign above reads POWER and the now-serving card shows 3, letters unchanged. The machine's lights blink softly. Same light throughout.
Natural documentary realism, soft overhead office light.
Thanks.

Locked-off camera, no zoom, no pan. The cashier sits behind the glass of the wooden counter, facing straight to camera: blonde bob wig over a navy balaclava with a white ring around the face and a red triangle over his left eye, on the right side of the frame. He has no mouth and makes no mouth movement. The black mesh top of the server cabinet fills the bottom of frame, its small lights blinking. He is still for a moment, then his chin rises slowly, a long look up at the machine, then his head lowers slowly back down, unimpressed. His gloved hands lift a few centimetres off the counter, palms half open, then settle back. Finally a small, tired tilt of the head, held until the end, as if to say it is in the wrong place. He keeps facing the camera the whole time; the white ring and the red triangle never move on the balaclava, the triangle stays on the right of frame. The sign above reads POWER and the now-serving card shows 3, unchanged. Same light throughout.
Natural documentary realism, soft overhead office light.
Thanks.

Locked-off camera, no zoom, no pan. Behind the glass at the wooden counter, the cashier in the blonde bob wig and navy balaclava with the white ring and the red triangle over his left eye (right of frame) faces the camera, his black-gloved hands on the small POSITION CLOSED sign on the counter ledge. He slides the sign the last few centimetres along the ledge, deliberately, lets go, and sits back in his chair, hands folding in front of him. On the right, the tall black server cabinet with its small screen reading DISCOUNT APPLIED stands close to the counter. Its fans visibly slow, their blades going from a blur to slowly turning, and its lights blink more slowly. Then it begins to roll backward on its castors, slowly and heavily, moving as one rigid upright box, sliding out of frame to the right until only the counter and the cashier remain, with the room behind the counter in view. The small sign reads POSITION CLOSED throughout, the screen reads DISCOUNT APPLIED while it is in view, and the carved sign above reads POWER. Same light throughout.
Natural documentary realism, soft overhead light.
Thanks.

Locked-off camera, no zoom, no pan. Behind the glass at the wooden counter, the cashier in the blonde bob wig and navy balaclava with the white ring and the red triangle over his left eye (right of frame) faces the camera. He pauses with his black-gloved hands on the POSITION CLOSED sign, then with one fingertip nudges it the last few centimetres across the ledge, small and precise. He leans back and rests his hands in his lap, perfectly still, still facing the camera. A beat later, on the right of frame, the tall black server cabinet with its small screen reading DISCOUNT APPLIED winds down: its fans slow to a lazy turn, its lights dim a little. It then reverses slowly on its castors, a heavy, smooth backward roll, staying rigid and upright, and drifts out of frame to the right. The counter, the carved wooden pillar and the POWER sign above stay exactly as they are; the small sign on the ledge reads POSITION CLOSED throughout and the screen reads DISCOUNT APPLIED while it is in view. Same light throughout.
Natural documentary realism, soft overhead light.
Thanks.

Locked-off camera, no zoom, no pan. On the left, the woman in the mustard coat stands at the wooden counter, her left hand steadying the white kettle on the counter, her right hand at the white wall socket below it on the right. She pushes the plug fully into the socket with a small firm press. A moment later a small light on the kettle's base glows on. Over the next few seconds the kettle begins to boil: a thin wisp of steam rises from the spout, builds, and then pours out in a steady white plume, curling up against the glass. She watches it and her face breaks into a warm, satisfied smile, mouth closed. Behind the glass, the cashier in the blonde bob wig and navy balaclava with the white ring and the red triangle over his left eye (right of frame) faces the camera with gloved hands folded on the counter, and gives a single small nod, then stays still. The ring and triangle never move. The carved sign above reads POWER, unchanged. Same light throughout.
Natural documentary realism, soft daylight.
Thanks.

Locked-off camera, no zoom, no pan. On the left, the woman in the mustard coat holds the white kettle on the wooden counter with her left hand while her right hand presses the plug the last little way into the white wall socket below. The small light on the kettle base comes on at once. She keeps her hand on the kettle and waits, glancing at it. Steam starts faintly from the spout, then thickens quickly and rolls out in a generous white cloud that drifts up toward the glass. As the steam pours, she smiles, a quiet, pleased smile, mouth closed, and lets go of the kettle. Behind the glass, the cashier in the blonde bob wig and navy balaclava with the white ring and the red triangle over his left eye (right of frame) stays facing the camera, gloved hands folded, and near the end gives one small, approving nod. The ring and triangle stay fixed. The carved sign above reads POWER, unchanged. Same light throughout.
Natural documentary realism, soft daylight.
Thanks.

Locked-off camera, no zoom, no pan. The red-haired lad in the grey hoodie stands beside the tall black server cabinet on the right of frame, his phone held against his chest in his left hand, his right hand at the small socket on the side of the cabinet holding the white cable plug. He is already looking back over his right shoulder toward the counters. He pushes the plug firmly into the socket, his eyes still darting back across the hall to check nobody saw. Holding that look for a beat, he then turns his head back to the cabinet, glances down at the plug, and a tiny, satisfied smile creeps onto his face, mouth closed. The cabinet's green and blue lights keep blinking. The people at the distant counters stay where they are, going about their business. The POWER signs keep their exact letters. Same three-quarter view of him, same light throughout.
Natural documentary realism, overcast daylight.
Thanks.

Locked-off camera, no zoom, no pan. The red-haired lad in the grey hoodie stands beside the tall black server cabinet on the right of frame, phone pressed to his chest in his left hand, his right hand at the small socket on the cabinet's side with the white cable plug. He is looking back over his shoulder toward the counters. He turns his head back toward the cabinet, slides the plug home into the socket with a small push of effort, then quickly glances back over his shoulder a second time, eyes narrowed, checking the hall. Nobody looks his way. He turns back, lets out a slow breath, and the corner of his mouth lifts into a tiny, smug smile, mouth closed. The cabinet lights keep blinking green and blue. The people at the distant counters stay where they are. The POWER signs keep their exact letters. Same light throughout.
Natural documentary realism, overcast daylight.
Thanks.

Locked-off camera, no zoom, no pan. Almost a still frame. A hand in a grey sleeve holds a black phone upright in the centre of frame, the white charging cable hanging down from its base, the blurred hall behind it. The hand barely moves, the slightest natural tremor. On the black screen, the thin white ring in the middle slowly grows brighter over the whole eight seconds, from a soft grey-white to a clean, bright white with a faint glow, staying exactly the same size, shape and position. The rest of the screen stays pure black. The blurred background stays soft and still. Same light throughout.
Quiet, natural realism, shallow depth of field.
Thanks.

Locked-off camera, no zoom, no pan. Almost a still frame. A hand in a grey sleeve holds a black phone upright in the centre of frame, white cable hanging from its base, the hall a soft blur behind. For the first two seconds nothing changes. Then the thin white ring in the middle of the black screen begins to brighten, gently and evenly, until by the end it is a crisp, luminous white ring with a faint soft glow around it, the same size and in the same place. The rest of the screen remains pure black. The hand stays almost perfectly still, the thumb shifting a millimetre at most. The blurred background stays soft. Same light throughout.
Quiet, natural realism, shallow depth of field.
Thanks.
